entry.title: Review: Woodo - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition - An Irresistible, Hard-To-Define Formula For Pure Relaxation
entry.summary: Could-o Woodo should-o. Woodo is like a cosy colouring book – that’s how three-person indie studio Tiny Monks Tales characterises its game. You have the outline of a colourless scene and need to beautify it by applying colourful items in the right places. This is a good comparison and one that captures the mindful focus and something-do-to-while-doing-something-else-ness of colouring in. But Woodo isn’t really a colouring book. Its scenes do begin as muted, almost ghostly dioramas, with each object you place painting another little patch of life into them. However, there’s no choice of what colour goes where and no risk of going over the lines. Instead, the pieces are rendered as gorgeous little chunks of wood, painted and varnished, that slot into their predefined homes. There’s something particularly satisfying about watching a grey, indistinct space become a warm, detailed, wooden world one piece at a time. Read the full article on nintendolife.com

entry.title: Paradox's grand strategy game Afterworld hasn't got a fixed history, it changes with every playthrough
entry.summary: Each time you start a new campaign in Afterworld, Paradox's upcoming post-apocalyptic grand strategy game, a tiny virtual historian cracks their knuckles and gets to work writing a new 200-year history for what happened to North America in the dying days of the great war. They will decide where the great powers fired their nuclear-tipped missiles, where they released their clouds of flesh-eating nanites, where they dropped their lung-bubbling chemical weapons, and they will decide who survived and who died. These procedural changes should mean that each time you start a new game of Afterworld, the map will be dramatically different from the last. That flexibility to rewrite the surface of Afterworld is vital, game director Dan Lind tells me, "Otherwise it undermines a lot of the exploration". Read more

entry.title: New horror game The Well Is Not Empty combines photophobic monsters with timer light switches and a lot of frenzied digging
entry.summary: "Never show the monster," horror film-makers, game-makers and other creepozoids have chanted, over the decades. The Well Is Not Empty wastes no time showing us the monster - one of the monsters, at least - and doesn't seem especially the worse for it. I mean, it's the worse, but in a good way. Look, you can see the monster right there, hunkered up like a frightened puppy in the corner of the room. A scrawny little fellow with broken xylophone teeth and eyes that genuinely do make me think of the view from the bottom of a well. The monster is no threat, as long as you stay out of grabbing distance - and as long as the lights are on. The problem, as you've already guessed, is that the lights are unreliable.
